title: The mikveh
hookLine: a pool of natural water for ritual immersion

lines: A SMALL POOL, A QUIET DOOR.
cards: In the first chapter of Genesis, the waters are gathered into one place and dry land appears. Then God names them, in the old JPS translation: "the gathering together of the waters called He Seas."
The Hebrew behind that gathering is mikveh.
The same word names something much smaller today: a pool, often in a quiet building with a discreet door, where a person walks down a few steps into water, goes under, and comes back up.

teach.h: GATHERED BY RAIN OR SPRING, NOT BUCKETS.
teach.b: Mikveh. A gathering of water. First, what kind of water.
A mikveh isn't filled from a tap like a bathtub. The Mishnah's tractate Mikvaot insists the water be gathered the way the world gathers it: rain, or a spring, not carried in by hand in buckets.

Second, a ladder. The tractate opens by ranking gatherings of water, from a shallow puddle upward, each fit for more than the one below. At the top: mayim chayim, living waters, water that flows from its source.
The Torah uses that phrase in its purity laws, and the rabbis hear in it water that is alive, still moving.
Third, who goes in. In traditional practice, a person becoming a Jew immerses in a mikveh. So do brides before their wedding.
Some men go before Shabbat or Yom Kippur. New dishes can be dipped too. And married women who keep the laws of family purity immerse monthly, which is tomorrow's subject.
Fourth, a play on words from Rabbi Akiva. The prophet Jeremiah calls God, in the old JPS translation, "O LORD, the hope of Israel." In Hebrew, hope there is mikveh.

teach.h: AKIVA: GOD, THE MIKVEH OF ISRAEL.
teach.b: So, says Rabbi Akiva in the Mishnah, God is the mikveh of Israel: just as a mikveh makes the impure pure, so God makes Israel pure.
The pool in the basement and the hope of a nation share a word.

how: In traditional practice, people converting to Judaism immerse in a mikveh, and some brides, married women, men before holy days, and new dishes are immersed too; Jewish communities differ on which of these they keep, and some have created new immersion customs.

o: a pool of gathered rain or spring water for immersion
the great bronze bowl where the Temple's priests washed

s: a mikveh is filled from the tap like a bath
its water has to be gathered the way the world gathers it: rain or a spring, not buckets.
the word mikveh appears in the creation story
the gathering together of the waters in Genesis is mikveh in Hebrew.
Rabbi Akiva read Jeremiah's word for hope as mikveh
as a mikveh makes the impure pure, he said, so God makes Israel pure.

games.q: you're reading Jeremiah with Rabbi Akiva: 'O LORD, the hope of Israel.' the Hebrew for hope is mikveh. what does he do with it?
o: translate it only as hope and move on.
read it as God, the mikveh of Israel, who purifies.
games.why: in the Mishnah, Rabbi Akiva says: just as a mikveh makes the impure pure, so God makes Israel pure.

practice: Fill a bowl or a sink, or hold your hands under a gently running tap, and lower them a little at a time, feeling the water climb past your knuckles and wrists.
At a mikveh, nothing is meant to come between the water and the skin, so let it touch everything. Then lift your hands out, let them drip, and notice the difference between before and after.

wordCard.voice: Mikveh. A gathering of water: a pool of rain or spring water for immersion, and in Jeremiah, a word for hope. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a gathering of water; in Jeremiah 17:13, hope.

carryVoice: Your line: living waters. Gathered, still moving, and a person coming up changed. Until tomorrow.
